clue.text: Assaulted while sleeping without Guardian

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside: the sleeping word goes round the newspaper's word

parts.note: abed means in bed, sleeping
the Guardian newspaper refers to itself as us, a convention of its own crosswords

explanation.surface: Someone was attacked in their sleep while the newspaper wasn't there to protect them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' means outside here, so ABED surrounds US. The Guardian setters use US for their own paper.
explanation.definitionFit: To be abused is to be mistreated or attacked, the same sense as assaulted.

clue.text: Report of forbidden group one can 18

indicators.note: a report is something heard, so the word for forbidden is taken by how it is spoken

parts.note: forbidden means banned

explanation.surface: News of a prohibited organisation that someone is able to defeat.
explanation.walkthrough: 18 is BEAT: the thematic clues each name something you can beat. 'To beat the band' is an idiom for doing something to the utmost.
explanation.definitionFit: A band is a musical group, and the idiom beat the band names it as something one can beat.

clue.text: Retiring to catch group of games in group of plants

indicators.note: catching something means holding it, so the retiring word encloses the games word

parts.note: retiring means bashful, shy
a rubber is a series of games, as in bridge or whist

explanation.surface: A shy person among sportsmen and a collection of plants.
explanation.definitionFit: A shrubbery is an area planted with bushes, a collection of plants.

clue.text: Make portrait of French inhabitant of Scotland

parts.note: de is the French word for of
the Picts were ancient inhabitants of Scotland

explanation.surface: Paint a likeness of a French-born Scot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'French' stands for the French word for 'of', which is DE.
explanation.definitionFit: To depict someone is to represent them in a picture, to portray them.

clue.text: Shoelaces from the last century

indicators.note: from signals that the answer is made out of these letters, rearranged

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, a century

explanation.surface: Laces for shoes that date back to the previous hundred years.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' is the anagram signal: THE, LAST and C rearrange. The surface wants 'the last century' to be a date.
explanation.definitionFit: A latchet is an old word for a thong or lace fastening a shoe, as in John's gospel.

clue.text: One can 18 them out of playwright Henry around end of tunnel

indicators.note: around says the playwright's surname goes round the tunnel's end

parts.note: Henry Livings was an English playwright
daylight is what is seen at the end of a tunnel

explanation.surface: Something to be thrashed out of a writer, wrapped round the light at a tunnel's end.
explanation.walkthrough: 18 is BEAT: 'to beat the living daylights out of' someone is to thrash them. 'around' wraps the playwright's surname round the tunnel's end.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom to beat the living daylights out of someone completes the definition, so the phrase is what is beaten out.

clue.text: Tumulus disturbed outside key Roman town

indicators.note: outside says the shuffled mound goes round the key
disturbed suggests the burial mound's letters are shaken up

parts.note: C is a musical key

explanation.surface: An ancient burial mound is dug up beyond a vital Roman settlement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disturbed' scrambles TUMULUS to TUSULUM; 'outside' puts that round C.
explanation.definitionFit: Tusculum was an ancient town in the Alban Hills near Rome.

clue.text: Clue to earth producing pulse

parts.note: the words ..., read as wordplay, would mean ... up ..., giving earth by rearrangement

explanation.surface: A hint about the soil that gives a throb.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: the answer read as a clue, 'heart' with 'beat' as anagram signal, makes EARTH. HEART is 7 and BEAT 18, the theme word.
explanation.definitionFit: A heartbeat is a single pulsation of the heart, a pulse.

clue.text: One can 18 yonder party

parts.note: yonder means over there
a treat is an outing or party given for others

explanation.surface: Something defeatable that lies over there, plus a celebration.
explanation.walkthrough: 18 is BEAT: armies 'beat the retreat', a drum ceremony at dusk.
explanation.definitionFit: Beating the retreat is a military drum ceremony, so the phrase names something one can beat.

clue.text: Soviet leader's article leading to sound sleep?

parts.note: an is the indefinite article

indicators.note: sound says the words for sleep are taken by how they are spoken

parts.note: to drop off is to fall asleep

explanation.surface: A Soviet leader's essay sends readers into deep slumber.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sound' looks like an adjective for 'sleep' but signals a homophone of DROP OFF; the question mark admits the stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: Yuri Andropov briefly led the Soviet Union after Brezhnev, in 1982 to 1984.

clue.text: 5 down can be out of the society minded

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for society
to have minded is to have cared

explanation.surface: A social club worries about losing its head.
explanation.walkthrough: 5 down is LIVING DAYLIGHTS: you can scare the living daylights out of someone, not only beat them out.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom scared the living daylights out of uses this word, completing the definition.

clue.text: Degree with qualification restricts snacks

parts.note: BA, Bachelor of Arts, is a degree
con is Italian and Spanish for with, as in musical directions
but introduces a qualification or reservation
ties means restricts or binds

explanation.surface: A graduate's diploma limits what they may eat between meals.
explanation.walkthrough: A BACON BUTTY is a British bacon sandwich. CON for 'with' comes from musical terms such as con brio.
explanation.definitionFit: Bacon butties are bacon sandwiches, quick food eaten as snacks.

clue.text: Some fun with boat, stocking it with liver, kidney etc (no heart)

indicators.note: stocking means filling, so the boat holds the other pieces

parts.note: a bark or barque is a sailing boat

indicators.note: no heart means one central letter is taken out of the organs word

parts.note: offal is the edible organs such as liver and kidney

explanation.surface: Amusement with a boat stocked with liver, kidneys and the like, but no heart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no heart' drops the middle letter of the organs word, giving OFAL; 'stocking' fills the boat. 'heart' looks like more offal, but it is the deletion signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A bit of a lark is a mild piece of fun or amusement.

clue.text: Enemy one can 18

definitions.meaning: the old enemy is a traditional nickname for passing ...
a musician can beat ..., keeping the rhythm

explanation.walkthrough: 18 is BEAT. 'How goes the enemy?' is an old way to ask the hour.
explanation.definitionFit: Time is the proverbial enemy, and a conductor or drummer beats time.

clue.text: Big shots going nonstop with what one can 18 and sack

parts.note: a drum is something you beat
to sack someone is to fire them

explanation.surface: Important people keep going with a beating and a dismissal.
explanation.walkthrough: 18 is BEAT. 'Big shots' looks like important people, but it means heavy artillery.
explanation.definitionFit: Drumfire is continuous massed artillery fire, heavy guns going without a pause.

clue.text: Weak in character but would then be truthful over the more important?

definitions.meaning: lacking moral fibre, so feeble in character

definitions.text: would then be truthful over the more important?
definitions.meaning: lie only about lesser things, so tell the truth about bigger ones

explanation.walkthrough: The second half is whimsical: the answer split as FIB RE LESS describes someone fibbing only about lesser matters.
explanation.definitionFit: Without fibre in the sense of moral strength, someone is weak in character.

clue.text: German turns up keeping a vehicle in grassland

indicators.note: keeping means holding, so the name goes round the other pieces
in a down clue turning up reads the German name from bottom to top

parts.note: Hans is a typical German man's name
a van is a vehicle

explanation.surface: A German shows up with a vehicle in a stretch of grassland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turns up' reverses the name to SNAH, which 'keeping' wraps round the article and vehicle.
explanation.definitionFit: A savannah is open tropical grassland with scattered trees.

clue.text: Excess of partners makes my play go wrong

indicators.note: going wrong suggests these words come out jumbled

explanation.surface: Too many spouses ruin my drama.
explanation.definitionFit: Polygamy is having more than one spouse at once, a surplus of partners.

clue.text: See 7
Springs one can 18

definitions.meaning: springs as a verb means leaps, jumps
beating the ... is an old English parish custom of walking its boundaries

explanation.walkthrough: 18 is BEAT. Beating the bounds is a parish procession marking its borders by striking them.
explanation.definitionFit: Bounds are leaps, and also the parish boundaries walked and struck in an old custom.

clue.text: Singer at fish bar — it's lunch time

parts.note: the bass is a fish
taken as written
the 's only shows possession or stands for 'is', so it adds no letters: the word before it gives these letters as it is written
one o'clock is a usual lunch hour

explanation.surface: A vocalist at a seafood counter announces it is time to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's of 'it's' is the link 'is': IT, then ONE for one o'clock.
explanation.definitionFit: A bass-baritone is a male singer whose range lies between bass and baritone.

clue.text: Bird, the satirist

explanation.walkthrough: The surface also hints at John Bird, a British satirist.
explanation.definitionFit: A swift is a bird, and Swift was the Irish satirist of Gulliver's Travels.

clue.text: Boy or girl, say, with share that was 18 in the '50s

parts.note: Gene is a first name for a boy, and the girl's Jean is said the same
a ration is a fixed share

explanation.surface: A child gets their portion, a group that was all the rage fifty years back.
explanation.walkthrough: 18 is BEAT: the Beat Generation was the circle of writers such as Kerouac and Ginsberg in the 1950s.
explanation.definitionFit: The Beat Generation was the 1950s literary movement, so this word completes the name.

clue.text: See 22
Baffled deer? Baffled deer

parts.note: a hind is a female deer

indicators.note: baffled here means confused, so the letters of the second deer are mixed up

explanation.surface: A deer is confused, and so is another deer.
explanation.walkthrough: The repetition looks like a stutter: first 'Baffled' defines, the first 'deer' gives HIND, then 'Baffled' scrambles DEER to ERED.
explanation.definitionFit: Hindered means obstructed or thwarted, as baffled does in its old sense of foiled.

clue.text: Drawings for first of several boats

indicators.note: first of picks the opening letter of several

parts.note: ketches are two-masted sailing boats

explanation.surface: Plans drawn up for the leading vessel of a fleet.
explanation.definitionFit: Sketches are rough drawings.

clue.text: Artist enclosed land in borders of Surrey

indicators.note: in says the island sits inside those letters
borders of takes the outermost letters of the county name

parts.note: an isle is land enclosed by water

explanation.surface: A painter fenced off a plot within the edges of a home county.
explanation.walkthrough: Alfred SISLEY was an English-born Impressionist. Surrey is a county south of London.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfred Sisley was an Impressionist painter, an artist.
